tldr: The authors propose a method that aligns an image encoder using features from a pretrained 3D point cloud model (Point-MAE) as a teacher only during training, accelerating policy convergence by up to 5.6x and boosting success rates while using only camera images during robot deployment.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. On the left, object point clouds are passed through a pretrained Point-MAE and mapped to 2D image patches via back-projection to construct alignment targets. On the right, a diffusion policy taking standard image inputs is trained, with an additional alignment loss pulling patch features toward Point-MAE's geometric features.
overview:
In robotic manipulation, 3D shape and geometric information are critical. Representations aware of 3D space help policies remain robust to viewpoint variations, object displacement, and occlusions. However, handling 3D point clouds or depth information on real robots creates major hurdles: adding depth cameras, precise calibration, and real-time point cloud compute overhead. Consequently, practitioners prefer policies that run purely on RGB camera images, but pure 2D images often lack a deep understanding of geometric structure.

To tackle this, the authors started with a question: Can an image-based policy acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment? They turned to representation alignment (REPA), an approach that guides intermediate features of a model using a pretrained representation. Extending this idea, they adopted a pretrained 3D self-supervised point cloud model, Point-MAE, as a "shape teacher." Point-MAE features are extracted from point clouds of object regions visible in the camera image, mapped onto image patches using camera projection geometry, and distilled into patch-level representations during training.

Experiments on the LIBERO simulation benchmark show that image encoders trained with this alignment learn strong correspondences across similar parts of different objects (such as bottle necks or bowl rims) and cleanly separate distinct object features. Furthermore, when fine-tuning pretrained policies, convergence is accelerated by up to 5.6x alongside improved success rates. It offers a practical way to inject geometric priors efficiently without altering the deployment pipeline or its computational footprint.
contributions: Proposed shape-teacher alignment, transferring 3D geometric structure into an image encoder during training while preserving a purely RGB image input interface at deployment.
Constructed an alignment algorithm that maps local features from a pretrained 3D point cloud encoder (Point-MAE) to individual image patches using camera back-projection and coverage weighting.
Demonstrated on the LIBERO benchmark that the method accelerates fine-tuning of pretrained models by up to 5.6x and learns advanced visual representations structured around shape and object parts.

sections.heading: Why teach 3D shape to a 2D image policy?
sections.summary: While geometric information is valuable for robotic manipulation, deploying 3D sensors is costly, making camera-only policies highly desirable. This section introduces the core idea: using a pretrained 3D shape model as a teacher only during training to align the image encoder, acquiring geometric structure without deployment-time overhead.
sections.details:
When a robot grasps or manipulates objects, capturing 3D shape and spatial layout provides a massive advantage. Policies incorporating 3D awareness are known to exhibit high sample efficiency and robustness against changes in viewpoint, object displacement, and occlusion. In practice, however, equipping physical robots with depth cameras, calibrating them accurately, and running real-time point cloud processing can lead to high costs and operational failures. Therefore, simple 2D policies that rely solely on RGB camera images remain the most attractive and convenient option.

Yet, pure 2D image policies face a dilemma: they struggle to grasp spatial geometry, often leading to manipulation failures. This motivated the authors' question: Can an image-based policy acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment?

Recently, representation alignment (REPA)—which aligns intermediate representations with features from a frozen pretrained encoder—has gained traction for stabilizing and speeding up diffusion model training. While prior robotics works have aligned policies using vision models like DINO, those align primarily with image "semantics" rather than explicit 3D geometry. In contrast, this paper proposes a novel framework using a pretrained 3D self-supervised point cloud model, Point-MAE, as a shape teacher to align image patch representations with geometric features.

sections.heading: How do you teach 3D point cloud features to 2D image patches?
sections.summary: After outlining the baseline diffusion policy, this section details the geometric alignment mechanism mapping local Point-MAE features to 2D image patches. Using back-projection and a coverage-weighted cosine similarity loss, training proceeds without altering the deployment pipeline at all.
sections.details:
### Baseline Diffusion Policy Setup
This work uses a diffusion policy as the baseline for behavior cloning. It receives consecutive images across two timesteps, $t-1$ and $t$, predicting a 10-step action trajectory and executing 8 of those steps. The observation encoder is a ViT/S-14 where, similar to DINOv2, the CLS token is discarded and the patch tokens are directly used as observation features. Language instructions are encoded with a frozen CLIP language model, diffusion timesteps are encoded with sinusoidal embeddings, and denoising is carried out via a 2-layer encoder and a 12-layer transformer decoder with cross-attention.

### Shape-Teacher Alignment
The core of the proposed method is how to map local 3D features from a frozen Point-MAE to individual 2D image patches. The procedure is as follows:

- Object point clouds are reconstructed using object masks and depth information from the training data, resampled to 1024 points, and partitioned into local groups of 32 points each.
- Each group is fed into Point-MAE to extract a 3D local feature $z_a^j$.
- 3D points are back-projected onto the image plane using camera parameters to calculate the coverage weight: the proportion of points in group $a$ falling within image patch $p$.
- These weights are used to compute a weighted average of the 3D group features, forming an alignment target vector for patch $p$.
- The image encoder's patch feature $f_p$ is passed through a small alignment head $h$, and a coverage-weighted cosine similarity loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$ is computed against the target vector.

The final training loss combines the standard behavior cloning loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}$ with the alignment loss weighted by $\lambda$ (default $\lambda=3$): $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$. Because the teacher is used only during training and discarded at deployment, it imposes no extra computation or sensor requirements during execution.

sections.heading: What did the aligned encoder learn, and how much faster did it become?
sections.summary: Using the LIBERO benchmark, the authors thoroughly evaluated the learned feature representations, policy convergence speed, and robustness to object displacement and occlusions. Fine-tuning pretrained models sped up convergence by up to 5.6x, revealing clear differences compared to a semantic teacher (DINOv2).
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial suites of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark. Models were evaluated under two regimes: training from scratch ("From Scratch") and fine-tuning weights pretrained on LIBERO-90 ("Pretrained").

### 3.1 Acquiring Shape- and Object-Centric Representations
To examine whether the image encoder acquired 3D geometric structure, patch-level cosine similarities were analyzed. When searching for patches most similar to a given query patch, the baseline tended to retrieve nearby patches on the same object or jump to unrelated areas. In contrast, the Point-MAE aligned model showed a dramatic increase in matching corresponding parts on differently shaped objects (increasing from 8.2% to 35.1% in pretrained models, and from 10.7% to 36.4% from scratch). For instance, geometrically similar parts like bottle necks or bowl rims were accurately matched. Additionally, t-SNE visualizations of mean object features revealed well-separated clusters for each object category, indicating that both part-level geometric structure and object-level grouping were acquired.

### 3.2 Drastic Acceleration of Policy Convergence
These representation changes translated directly into policy learning efficiency. Comparing training time to reach the baseline's final success rate, the pretrained model demonstrated impressive acceleration: 5.6x on LIBERO-Spatial and 4.7x on LIBERO-Object. In from-scratch training, it achieved 3.9x and 2.3x speedups, respectively. This shows that the alignment loss does not merely alter the final representations, but substantially improves the optimization trajectory itself.

### 3.3 Robustness to Environmental Variations
The authors tested policy robustness under annular object displacements (Displacement) and occlusions (LIBERO-Occ). While the shape-aligned model matched or exceeded baseline robustness, improvements were not uniformly dramatic across all variations, with performance gains varying depending on the task suite and perturbation type.

### 3.4 Teacher Model Comparison Ablation
The authors compared Point-MAE against a teacher offering strong 2D semantic representations: DINOv2 ($\lambda=1$). While DINOv2 alignment achieved very high task success rates in certain scenarios, the nature of the learned features was distinctly different. DINOv2 produced semantically driven representations that grouped the entire object together, whereas Point-MAE guided the encoder toward geometric representations recognizing shared structural parts across different objects. A key takeaway is that different inductive biases can be injected into the encoder depending on the chosen teacher.

sections.heading: Appendix: Robustness evaluation setup and alignment weight sweeps
sections.summary: This section covers the generation of the dual-ring displacement dataset used to evaluate out-of-distribution robustness and examines how the alignment loss weight affects convergence speed.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed supplementary information regarding the experiments.

### Construction of the Displacement Dataset
To evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) placement, two concentric rings (Ring 1 and Ring 2) were constructed around the target object's placement area in the original dataset. Based on the diameter of the original bounding box, Ring 1 was defined as 0.1 to 0.25 times the diameter from the edge, and Ring 2 as 0.35 to 0.50 times, with test locations sampled via rejection sampling. In LIBERO-Spatial, where variance was high, local outlier factor (LOF) filtering was applied to remove outliers before defining the regions.

### The Sweet Spot for Alignment Weight $\lambda$
Varying the alignment loss weight $\lambda$ revealed a sweet spot: setting the weight too high slowed convergence and harmed performance, particularly when training from scratch. Conversely, when fine-tuning pretrained models, performance degradation at higher weights was minimal, demonstrating consistent and robust gains.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: A summary of the effectiveness of shape-teacher alignment during training, followed by a discussion of limitations—such as reliance on a single architecture and simulation—and promising future directions.
sections.details:
This study established shape-teacher alignment, an approach that distills 3D geometric representations into policies during training while retaining a lightweight 2D image interface during deployment. On the LIBERO benchmark, policies developed visual representations structured around object shapes and corresponding parts, drastically accelerating training convergence. Moreover, comparing Point-MAE with a semantic teacher (DINOv2) showed that one can directly inject targeted inductive biases into the encoder by choosing the alignment target.

However, acknowledged limitations include restricting the experiments to a single policy architecture (Diffusion Policy) and the LIBERO simulation environment. In addition, only Point-MAE was explored as a shape teacher. Future work includes exploring multimodal 3D teachers combining geometry and semantics, as well as validating the approach on real-world robots under complex occlusions.

takeaways: Even when deploying 3D sensors is undesirable, 3D geometric structure can be safely distilled into 2D image policies by aligning patches with a point cloud teacher (Point-MAE) exclusively during training.
When fine-tuning pretrained policies, adding shape alignment substantially accelerates training convergence by roughly 4.7x to 5.6x.
Using DINOv2 (semantic-focused) versus Point-MAE (shape-focused) induces distinctly different biases in the encoder, highlighting the importance of choosing a teacher suited to task needs.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to simulation (LIBERO) and a specific diffusion policy architecture; real-world robot validation remains future work.
While shape alignment tends to improve resilience against displacement and occlusions, it does not uniformly deliver dramatic improvements across all types of distribution shifts.
Because the approach requires object segmentation masks and depth information for back-projection, 3D data remains essential for the training data collection pipeline.
